r: The course builds awareness of cultural values, traditions, and individual variation across communities and examines how a teacher's personal attitudes shape expectations and decisions in elementary, secondary, and special-education settings. The applied work is a candidate's interpersonal judgment with students, families, and colleagues plus reflective self-examination, activities task-exposure research places among the least automatable, since interpersonal and critical-reflection work is negatively associated with exposure. AI readily generates diversity readings, discussion cases, and reflection prompts, but it does not perform the relational competence the course cultivates. The binding constraint is institutional: this is a required component of a Colorado-approved educator-preparation program under SB 09-160, and the horizon assumes near-zero curricular restructuring. At 24 months the instrumental need for candidates to develop culturally responsive judgment is untouched; realized automatability is bounded and capability is simply not the operative variable here.

By 2031, AI tutoring and content tools will routinely supply multicultural curricular material, generate classroom scenarios, and draft reflective scaffolds, automating much of the course's information layer. What survives is the candidate's own capacity to read a class, weigh family and community context, and adjust instruction in real time, presence-dependent judgment with child-welfare stakes that keeps a knowledgeable human in the loop, echoing the jagged-frontier finding that uncritical trust in model output degrades accuracy. The Colorado approved-program mandate does not restructure within a catalog cycle or two, so the course stays locked into the licensure pathway. The instrumental case is preserved by that institutional lock and the interpersonal core together; AI shifts what candidates learn to oversee, including culturally flat or biased AI outputs, not whether they must develop the underlying dispositions the course targets.

A decade out, AI will deliver sophisticated, personalized diversity content and could reshape how the subject is taught. Here the institutional cap relaxes at the long horizon, since accreditors and the state could plausibly revise how this competency is delivered by 2036, so the rating rises to Medium rather than holding Low. Yet the embodied, relational heart of culturally responsive teaching, and candidates' need to detect when an AI system stereotypes or flattens learners, resist direct substitution. The genuine uncertainty is pedagogical and regulatory: how much awareness-building migrates to AI-mediated delivery, not whether the dispositional competence remains instrumentally needed. Rating Medium, reflecting an exposure of the execution layer that the licensure clock only stops capping at the ten-year mark, with the interpersonal core still doing meaningful protective work against full substitution.
ALP 2200.d: This course is designed to increase student awareness of the values and beliefs, traditions, identifiers, and contributions of African Americans, Asian Americans, Hispanic Americans, and Native Americans. Historical, cultural, and individual variations, including socio-economic status, gender, sexual orientation, language background and disabilities will be investigated to help develop respect for all students, parents, and educators in school settings. Students will discover how personal attitudes may affect expectations and decisions in the elementary, secondary, and special education school settings.

r: ALP 3600 introduces classroom exceptionality from an educational decision-making stance, using a case-study method in which candidates apply content to instructional problems calibrated to their early-childhood, elementary, or secondary licensure level. The applied work is professional judgment about instructing diverse learners with disabilities and giftedness, the kind of decision-heavy, critical-thinking task that task-exposure research finds negatively associated with AI exposure, even though drafting written case responses is a more exposed office task. AI can generate case analyses and suggest accommodations, but it does not exercise the situated instructional judgment about real learners that the course develops. The binding constraint is the Colorado-approved preparation program under SB 09-160, of which this is a required component. At 24 months, with negligible curricular change and adoption still diffusing, the instrumental need for candidates to reason through instructional decisions is essentially intact.

By 2031, AI systems will competently draft case analyses, propose differentiated accommodations, and surface disability-specific strategies, meaningfully augmenting how candidates prepare. The residual competence is deciding which recommendation fits a specific child and recognizing when a plausible AI suggestion is wrong, a verification burden with real, non-obvious costs given that a poor instructional decision for a student with a disability harms the learner. This is exactly the jagged-frontier condition that keeps knowledgeable humans necessary. The approved-program mandate does not relax within a catalog cycle, so the course remains required regardless of how automatable case write-ups become. The instrumental case is held at Low by institutional lock-in and by decision-verification stakes; AI changes the inputs to the candidate's judgment, not the requirement that the candidate be able to exercise it.

A decade out, AI decision-support for instructional planning will be pervasive and strong, and the case-drafting rationale is substantially eroded. The licensure cap relaxes only at this horizon, so the rating rises to Medium: accreditors could revise how decision-making competency is assessed, and much of the analytical shell automates. What resists substitution is the human judgment to individualize for a particular child and to catch a confidently wrong model recommendation before it reaches a vulnerable learner. The honest uncertainty is how special-education methods are taught and evaluated under ubiquitous AI, not whether candidates still need the underlying decision competence, which in the central case they do. Rating Medium, capped from higher by the residual verification role and from lower only because the mandate stops binding at ten years.
ALP 3600.d: ALP 3600 was designed to introduce students to exceptionality in the classroom from an educational decision- making perspective. Information regarding disabilities and giftedness is presented in a manner to familiarize students with the many instructional decisions they must be prepared to make on the basis of the diversity of the classroom population. The case study method is the approach that will be used in this course. Students will be expected to apply course content to solve various problems that are presented within the context of case studies. These case studies will be specific to the student's level of teacher licensure and will provide exposure to relevant issues pertaining to early childhood, elementary, or secondary education.

r: The course centers on Individualized Education Plans and transition plans, preparing special educators to write and implement curricula across special and general classrooms, with an overview of the foundations of education. The core applied task, drafting compliant IEP goals, services, and transition documentation, is precisely the structured writing-and-office work that observed-usage data shows AI performing well and that task-exposure research classifies as positively associated with exposure, so realized automatability is comparatively high here. But IEPs are legally binding documents with compliance stakes, creating a genuine verification burden, and the course is a required component of the Colorado-approved program under SB 09-160. At 24 months, AI already drafts serviceable IEP language, yet candidates must still learn to construct legally sound, individualized plans and to supervise automated drafts. The mandate and error-cost hold the instrumental case at Low.

By 2031, AI tools will draft IEP goals, generate present-levels narratives, and assemble transition plans from student data with facility, substantially automating the document-production the course teaches. The instrumental case shifts from writing plans to reviewing, individualizing, and legally validating them, a verification competence that grows more important as models produce fluent but occasionally non-compliant or ill-fitted output, consistent with jagged-frontier evidence. The approved-program requirement does not restructure within a catalog cycle, and IDEA-driven compliance keeps a knowledgeable human accountable for each plan. The rating stays Low: capability outruns institutional change, but the licensure architecture continues to require the competence. AI mediates the paperwork; the candidate remains responsible for whether an individualized plan actually serves the child and withstands legal scrutiny.

A decade out, AI will generate compliant, individualized IEP and transition drafts routinely, and the plan-authoring rationale is largely eroded, the clearest high-exposure element in this course. The licensure cap relaxes only now, lifting the rating to Medium as accreditors could revise how the competency is delivered and most drafting automates. The durable residue is human accountability: verifying legal sufficiency, individualizing to a specific learner, and detecting a confidently wrong plan before services are misdirected. Uncertainty is real about how much oversight the profession retains once AI drafts are trusted, which tempers confidence. Rating Medium, reflecting an execution layer that is among the more automatable in the batch, held from higher by the accountability-verification role and from lower because the mandate ceases to bind at the ten-year horizon.
ALP 3650.d: This course focuses on Individualized Education Plans (IEP) and transition plans for purposes of preparing special educators for teaching curricula within the context of special and general education classrooms. An overview of the philosophical, historical, and sociological foundations of education will be addressed.

r: Building on ALP 3650, this course develops transition services for students with exceptionalities from childhood to adulthood, covering transition-focused IEP development, self-determination and self-advocacy, inter-agency collaboration, transition assessment, and career, vocational, and postsecondary strategies. At 24 months, with adoption still diffusing across schools, the instrumental need to prepare candidates to orchestrate real transition services is intact.

By 2031, AI will draft transition-focused IEPs, match students to postsecondary and vocational pathways, and summarize transition assessments, offloading much documentation and information-gathering. The competence that survives is relational and coordinative: brokering agreements across schools, agencies, families, and employers, and coaching students in self-advocacy, work that is presence-dependent and not performed by a model. Errors in a transition plan carry consequential, non-obvious downstream effects on a young adult's trajectory, sustaining a real verification burden. The approved-program mandate does not relax within a catalog cycle, keeping this course fixed in the licensure sequence. The instrumental case remains Low; AI increasingly supplies the plan scaffolding while candidates retain responsibility for the human coordination and judgment the transition process actually turns on.

A decade out, AI will competently generate transition documentation, assessments, and service recommendations, and the paperwork rationale substantially erodes. The licensure cap relaxes at this horizon, so the rating rises to Medium as accreditors could revise delivery and most documentation automates. What resists substitution is the inter-agency coordination and the cultivation of student self-determination, embodied, relational work that remains necessary in the central case, alongside human accountability for verifying AI-generated plans against a real young person's needs. The uncertainty is how heavily AI mediates transition planning and how much coordination remains human, not whether the competence is still needed. Rating Medium, capped from higher by the durable interpersonal and verification core and from lower only because the SB 09-160 mandate stops binding at ten years.
ALP 3675.d: This course provides an in-depth understanding of transition services for students with exceptionalities from childhood to adulthood. Course content focuses on an in-depth investigation of the provision of transition services in the context of comprehensive, secondary education services. Topics in this course include transition-focused IEP development, self-determination and self- advocacy, inter-agency collaboration, transition assessment, and career, vocational, and post-secondary education strategies. Teacher candidates gain the knowledge base and skills necessary to successfully manage the transition services of their future students.

r: The course surveys the multidisciplinary needs of students with physical, communicative, cognitive, and sensory disabilities, emphasizes how medical needs shape educational experiences, addresses Universal Design for Learning, and requires a 15-hour field experience in a school serving students with severe disabilities. The binding constraint is a hard institutional lock: those supervised field hours count toward Colorado's mandated educator-preparation field-hour total under SB 09-160, with CAEP clinical-practice expectations layered on, and cannot be satisfied by an AI system. At 24 months the instrumental need for supervised practice is untouched.

By 2031, AI will fluently explain disability profiles and medical-educational implications and draft UDL adaptations, automating much of the didactic content. But the field component exists to develop a candidate's embodied competence supporting and instructing students with significant disabilities under supervision, a presence-dependent, high-stakes activity no model performs. Child-welfare and medical-adjacent error costs keep the verification burden real and the knowledgeable human in the room. The Colorado field-hour mandate does not change within a catalog cycle, so the placement requirement holds regardless of how automatable the knowledge layer becomes. The instrumental case is preserved by embodiment and licensure lock-in together; AI changes what candidates learn to interpret and oversee, not whether they must accumulate supervised in-person experience with these learners.

A decade out, AI will deliver authoritative disability-and-medical content and personalized UDL guidance, substantially eroding the information-transmission rationale. What remains necessary is the embodied field experience with students who have severe disabilities and the human judgment to apply and verify AI-mediated supports in a real classroom, competence that does not transfer to a model. Rating Medium, held from higher by the embodied field core and from lower only because the field-hour mandate stops being certain to bind by 2036.
ALP 3700.d: This course provides an overview of the multidisciplinary needs of students with physical, communicative, cognitive, and sensory disabilities. Emphasis is placed on explaining the impact of medical needs on educational experiences. Principles of Universal Design for Learning (UDL) will be addressed. Teacher candidates must complete a 15-hour field experience in an assigned public school that provides services for students with severe disabilities.

r: This course introduces assessment, curriculum, and instruction for students with severe disabilities, emphasizing inclusion in neighborhood schools, homework, and community, and the selection and efficacy of assistive device technologies, with a minimum 45-hour field-based experience. Although assistive-technology matching and assessment scoring are partly exposed analytical tasks, the substantial field hours put candidates in sustained, hands-on instructional contact with students who have severe disabilities, physical and interpersonal care that task-exposure research and observed-usage data place among the least automatable categories. AI can suggest an assistive device or tabulate assessment data, but it cannot position a student, adapt a task in the moment, or exercise the embodied instructional judgment the placement develops. The binding constraint is Colorado's mandated field hours under SB 09-160. At 24 months the instrumental need for this supervised, embodied practice is fully intact.

By 2031, AI will improve assistive-technology recommendation and automate more of the assessment and progress-monitoring analysis, augmenting how candidates plan. But the core of the course, developing competent hands-on technique and real-time instructional judgment for students with severe disabilities across school and community settings, is embodied and presence-dependent, and the 45 field hours cannot be delegated to a model. Verification stakes are high because these learners are vulnerable and failure modes are non-obvious, so the candidate must be able to judge whether a device match or data reading is actually right. The field-hour mandate does not relax within a catalog cycle, and community-based inclusion work keeps the placement in physical settings a model cannot enter. The instrumental case remains Low, protected by embodiment and licensure together; AI absorbs some analytical shell around a still-human instructional practice, not the practice itself.

Even with a decade of capability growth and broad classroom AI adoption, the requirement that candidates accumulate supervised in-person hours instructing students with severe disabilities is among the most durable constraints in this batch, and there is no central-case path to its removal by 2036. The embodied, care-intensive nature of the work resists direct substitution, and AI-mediated assistive tech raises rather than removes the need for a human who can judge fit and catch errors for a vulnerable learner. The genuine uncertainty is how much assessment and device-selection analysis automates, not whether the field experience remains necessary. Rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored by embodiment and the field-hour mandate, which the ten-year cap relaxation does not lift because the dampened base already sits at Low.
ALP 3750.d: This course is designed to introduce pre-service teachers to assessment, curriculum and instruction for students with severe disabilities. Focus will be given to including students in their neighborhood schools, homework, and community. The course also emphasizes the selection and efficacy of assistive device technologies. A minimum 45-hour, field-based experience is required.

r: The course covers the components of literacy, phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension, and teaches candidates to use assessment data to design lessons and apply scientifically-based interventions for students with literacy challenges including dyslexia, with a direct-instruction emphasis and a co-requisite 45-hour field class. ALP 3820.d: Within this course, students will learn about the components of literacy with a focus on phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension as taught in elementary classrooms. Assessment data is used to design lesson plans and apply scientifically-based interventions to address the needs of students with literacy challenges, including dyslexia. A direct-instruction teaching approach based on best practices is a focus. The course has a co-requisite of a field-based class which will includes a 45-hour field- based experience with elementary level students.

The uncertainty is how math methods are taught under ubiquitous AI solvers, not whether the teaching-and-verification competence remains required. Rating Medium, capped from higher by the interpersonal instructional core and from lower only because the field-hour mandate stops binding at the ten-year horizon.
ALP 3950.d: This course is designed to introduce effective classroom methods and strategies for teaching, assessing, and monitoring the mathematical performance of students with disabilities within diverse classroom settings. An emphasis is placed on practical classroom techniques to facilitate, maintain, retain, and generalize skill acquisition. Computation and problem-solving techniques are covered. This class requires a 15-hour, project-based field experience.
